Rust is a general-purpose programming language that emphasizes performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety [1]. Memory safety sits at the heart of its design.

### Origins

Graydon Hoare began developing Rust in 2006, and Mozilla Research later sponsored and maintained it from 2009 [2]. The language was first publicly released in 2010, and version 1.0 followed in 2015 [2].

### What Memory Safety Means

Memory safety protects programs from bugs and vulnerabilities in memory access, such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers [3]. C, C++, and Fortran allow arbitrary pointer arithmetic without bounds checking, which makes them memory-unsafe [3]. Java, by contrast, is memory-safe because its runtime checks array bounds and pointer dereferences [3].

### How Rust Pursues Safety

Rust is syntactically similar to C++, yet it guarantees memory safety without a garbage collector [2]. It also draws on functional programming ideas such as immutability and pattern matching [1].

### Conclusion

Rust occupies a distinctive position between C++-style performance and the guarantees of memory-safe languages.
